Notation and references

Adeles
A compatible list of local entries, one in each completion of a number field, integral at all but finitely many finite places. The diagonal embedding sends one field element to its value in every completion. Read in context
Almost everywhere
A property holds almost everywhere if the set where it fails has measure zero. Two functions in L² can differ on such a set and still represent the same vector. Read in context
Analytic continuation
An extension agreeing with a given analytic function on its original domain. Agreement on an open subset determines the continuation on a connected domain. Read in context
Annihilator
The characters of a finite abelian group that are identically one on a specified subgroup. Subgroup averaging selects exactly these characters. Read in context
Automorphic function
A function on an adelic group that descends under its rational subgroup and satisfies the prescribed regularity and other conditions. Square-integrability on the quotient matters for the lifts here. Read in context
Bar chain
A finite linear combination of ordered words in a group. Its boundary takes alternating faces obtained by omitting an end entry or multiplying neighboring entries. Read in context
Bernoulli value of a character
A weighted finite sum of Bernoulli polynomial values at fractions of the conductor. The minus estimate clears its denominators and uses the same algebraic integer at every coefficient prime. Read in context
Bockstein map
In the coefficient sequence for reduction modulo q, lift a cycle to an integral chain. Its boundary is a multiple of q. Dividing that boundary by q gives a class one degree lower, killed by q. This map distinguishes the two torsion orders in the cycle count. Read in context
Character / χ
A homomorphism from a finite group to nonzero complex numbers. A Dirichlet character extends by zero off the units modulo N. Read in context
Class group / Cl(K)
Fractional ideals of the number field K modulo principal fractional ideals. The quotient Cl(K)/ℓCl(K) measures the number of independent characters of order ℓ. Read in context
CM field
A number field that is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field. Complex conjugation interchanges the two embeddings over any real place of the base. Read in context
Cocycle
A function c satisfying c(gh)=c(g)+g·c(h). Its class in degree one identifies functions differing by g↦g·a−a. Local conditions impose restrictions on these classes. Read in context
Cocycle test on a prism
A linear functional that vanishes on boundaries. For the residue test, consecutive pairs contribute carries and the last entry contributes an additive index. Read in context
Coinvariants
Given an operator g on a module M, the quotient M/(g−1)M identifies each element with its translate under g. The quotient by gᵈ−1 maps onto it because gᵈ−1 is divisible by g−1. Read in context
Conductor / f
The least divisor of the modulus from which a Dirichlet character is induced. A primitive character has conductor equal to its modulus. Read in context
Covolume
The volume of a fundamental parallelepiped of a lattice in its real span with the chosen metric. Read in context
Critical strip / σ
The region 0 < Re s < 1. Here s = σ+it; σ = ½ is the critical line. Read in context
Cyclotomic layer
A stage in a tower formed by adjoining roots of unity. In the ℓ-adic tower here, layer m has relative degree ℓᵐ over the chosen base field. Read in context
Discrete valuation ring
A ring in which each nonzero element has the form uπⁿ for a unit u, a fixed uniformizer π and a nonnegative integer n. This exponent measures divisibility. For ℤℓ one can take π=ℓ. Read in context
Double coset
For subgroups Γ and K of a group, the double coset of h consists of the products γhk with γ in Γ and k in K. Grouping an integral by these classes preserves the measure of each class. Read in context
Doubling integral
An integral obtained by placing two copies of a unitary group in a larger group and pairing a section there with matrix coefficients on the original copies. Its local factors determine the partial L-function in the theta norm. Read in context
Elementary divisors
A pair of full local lattices can be put into diagonal form by integral changes of bases. The integer exponents of a uniformizer classify their relative position. Their sum gives the determinant valuation and the sum of their absolute values gives the degree in the split-place series. Read in context
Euler’s constant / γ
The limit of 1+1/2+⋯+1/n − log n; it is the constant Laurent coefficient of ζ at 1. Read in context
Field norm and ideal norm
In a Galois extension the field norm multiplies all conjugates of an element. The ideal norm sends a prime above a base prime to the power of the base prime given by the relative residue degree. For a principal ideal these two constructions agree. Read in context
Formal degree
The positive constant in Schur orthogonality for a discrete series and a chosen Haar measure. For a unit vector v it satisfies ∫|⟨v,σ(g)v⟩|² dg = 1/dσ. Read in context
Formal group and formal logarithm
A group law in power series at the identity and a change of coordinate taking that law to addition. Read in context
Frobenius and inertia
Inertia is the subgroup of a local Galois group acting trivially on the residue field. A Frobenius class acts there by raising to the residue-field size. Read in context
Genus mass
For a positive definite lattice, sum 1/|Aut(L)| over one representative of each isometry class in its genus. A weighted average of a count divides the corresponding weighted sum by this mass. Read in context
Gram matrix
The matrix of pairwise inner products of a list of vectors. Its diagonal records squared lengths. If the vectors are columns of M in orthonormal coordinates, the Gram matrix is M* M. Read in context
Haar measure
A translation-invariant measure on a locally compact group. Its normalization matters when comparing the two sides of the Petersson identity. Read in context
Hecke operator
An operator formed by summing translates indexed by the cosets in a double coset. The operator in the invariant-period comparison divides by the number of cosets, so it fixes constants. Read in context
Homology and cohomology
A cycle is a chain with zero boundary, and its homology class records it up to addition of boundaries. A cohomology class tests cycles by a cocycle, which vanishes on boundaries. Torsion counts and bounds on the dimension over the reals give different information. Read in context
Jacobi sum
For two multiplicative characters of a finite field, extended by zero at zero, sum χ(x)φ(1−x) over the field. In the nondegenerate cyclotomic case the product with the inverse-character sum is the size of the field. Read in context
Matrix coefficient
The scalar formed by translating one vector by a group element and pairing it with a second vector. When the vectors coincide, its value at the identity is their squared norm. Read in context
Mellin transform
Here the integral from 1 to infinity against x^(−s−1) dx. Under x=eᵘ it becomes a Laplace transform. Read in context
Module length
Number of simple quotients in a composition series. For a finite ℤℓ-module of order ℓᵈ the length is d. Its minimum number of generators can be smaller. Read in context
Mollifier for an L-function
A short Dirichlet polynomial chosen to cancel the early coefficients of a product with the L-series. Here its weights are μ(d)χ(d), where μ is the Möbius function. A zero forces the product of the two truncated sums to be small. Read in context
Moving frame
An identification of tangent spaces used to compare a form at different points. In the cone of positive Hermitian matrices, the action carrying the identity to a point pulls the form back to a tensor at the identity. Read in context
Multiplicity / m
At an isolated zero ρ, the integer m≥1 such that L(s)=(s−ρ)ᵐh(s) with h holomorphic and h(ρ)≠0. The balance chapter also uses m for a chain length. Read in context
Partition of unity
A collection of smooth nonnegative weights that add to one, with only finitely many nonzero in a neighborhood of each point. Here the weights index translates by the arithmetic group. Read in context
Period of an automorphic form
An integral of an automorphic function over a specified quotient, often after restricting the function to a subgroup or pairing it with a second function. The bottom period here restricts a core function to the row group and integrates their product. Read in context
Petersson pairing
The integral of the product of an automorphic function and the complex conjugate of another on the automorphic quotient, with the chosen measure. On the diagonal it gives a squared norm. Read in context
Poincaré series
A sum of translates of a test function over a discrete group or a coset space. The sum used to separate a row has an identity contribution large enough to dominate the sum of the other contributions after unfolding its period. Read in context
Pole and residue
The residue is the coefficient of (s−ρ)⁻¹ in a Laurent expansion. A simple pole has a nonzero residue and no higher-order singular terms. Read in context
Positive part / u₊
The number max(u,0). In a ramp it cuts off the sum; in the window estimate it keeps the side controlled by the hypothesis. Read in context
Ramification index
The multiplicity of a prime in the extended prime ideal. It enters the weighting of the finite-place contributions to divisibility. Read in context
Residue degree
The degree of an extension of residue fields. In an unramified quadratic extension, a split base prime has two primes of residue degree one. An inert prime has one of degree two. Read in context
Satake parameters
The unramified eigenvalue data that encode the action of the spherical Hecke operators at one place. The normalization used here specifies their powers of the residue-field size in the local Euler factors. Read in context
Saturation of a lattice
The saturation of Λ in E is the set of x in E such that kx lies in Λ for some nonzero integer k. Modulo Λ it gives exactly the torsion subgroup of E/Λ. Read in context
Semisimple representation
A direct sum of irreducible representations. One can compare multiplicities constituent by constituent once an isomorphism of the global representations has been established. Read in context
Sha-type local kernel
The subgroup of degree-one Galois cohomology classes whose restrictions at the specified places vanish. Its module length enters the cohomological window bound. Read in context
Shapiro’s isomorphism
Homology with an induced coefficient module can be computed in the subgroup. Here the module of functions on a finite cyclic quotient turns a homology calculation for G into one for the kernel. Read in context
Siegel parabolic
The subgroup preserving a maximal isotropic subspace in the doubled Hermitian space. Its rational cosets index the Eisenstein series used to identify the normalized theta mean. Read in context
Signature of a real unit
The signs of a unit at all real embeddings. Recording a negative value as one and a positive value as zero turns multiplication of units into addition of bit vectors. Read in context
Similitude
An invertible linear map that multiplies a Hermitian form by a single nonzero scalar. It sends the sphere of one length to the sphere of the scaled length. Read in context
Slope
For a Euclidean lattice of positive rank, its Arakelov slope is the negative log of its covolume divided by its rank. Extremal slopes measure sublattices and quotients. Read in context
Spherical data
At a good finite place the vectors are fixed by the specified maximal compact subgroup. This invariance permits the local integral to be evaluated by Hecke eigenvalues. Read in context
Split sequence
An ordered list of vectors vᵢ with specified linear functionals λᵢ satisfying λᵢ(vⱼ)=1 when i=j and 0 otherwise. Deleting one pair gives a shorter sequence. Read in context
Stabilizer
The subgroup of symmetries that take an object to itself. In the arithmetic face count a finite stabilizer acts faithfully on a finite set of shortest vectors. Its order contributes to the bound for integral homology. Read in context
Stickelberger element
An element of a group ring acting on ideal classes in cyclotomic arithmetic. Its annihilation property supplies a relation on a quotient of the class group in the tower argument. Read in context
Successive minima
For a lattice in a Euclidean space, the jth successive minimum is the least radius of a ball about zero containing j real-linearly independent lattice vectors. In the number-field row argument, independence over the field requires taking the radii in blocks. Read in context
Target slice
For a kernel K(x,y) and a fixed source point x, the function y ↦ K(x,y) on the target. Its square-integral as x varies controls the change of integration order in the theta pairing. Read in context
Tate twist
A change in a Galois action by a power of the cyclotomic character, which records the action on roots of unity. Its exponent matters in a local restriction kernel. Read in context
Theta lift
An integral operator with a theta kernel carrying an automorphic function between spaces for two groups. Read in context
Thick part
The region of positive Hermitian forms where both the primal and dual lattice minima are at least a fixed positive constant. A compact set meets every arithmetic orbit in this region. Read in context
Trace-dual basis
For a finite separable extension, bases (uᵢ) and (vⱼ) are trace-dual when Tr(uᵢvⱼ) is 1 for i=j and 0 otherwise. Then x=∑ᵢ Tr(xuᵢ)vᵢ. Clearing both bases at once produces the split residue calculation. Read in context
Valuation / vₚ
The exponent of p in a nonzero rational number, extended by vₚ(0)=+∞. The normalized p-adic absolute value is p to the power −vₚ. Read in context
Von Mangoldt function / Λ
Λ(pʲ)=log p for a prime p and integer j≥1; its value at every other positive integer is zero. Read in context
Whittaker coefficient
A Fourier coefficient obtained by integrating along a unipotent matrix variable against an additive character. In the Siegel–Weil calculation, a nonsingular Hermitian matrix specifies the character. At the special parameter the coefficient reads the density of tuples with that Gram matrix. Read in context
Window / Y, U, δ
An interval [Y,Y¹⁺ᵟ] with δ>0; in logarithmic coordinates its endpoints are U=log Y and (1+δ)U. Read in context
Witt index
Largest dimension of a subspace on which the entire Hermitian pairing vanishes. It determines which convergence hypothesis is required for the doubled theta integral. Read in context

Theorems used in the book

  1. The pole of the zeta function

    The series for ζ(s) on Re s > 1 extends meromorphically to the plane. At its only pole the expansion begins ζ(s) = 1/(s−1) + γ + O(s−1), where γ is Euler’s constant.

    Taking the logarithmic derivative of this expansion specifies the two centering terms in the smoothed prime sum.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §25.2(i) and (ii), especially (25.2.4).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2

    Used in From a series to a function · Why the correction terms have these signs

  2. Euler product for a Dirichlet character

    If χ is a Dirichlet character and Re s > 1, then L(s,χ) is the absolutely convergent product over primes p of (1−χ(p)p⁻ˢ)⁻¹. A prime dividing the modulus contributes the factor 1.

    Taking the logarithmic derivative turns each Euler factor into a sum over powers of its prime. That sum supplies the weights in the Mellin transform.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, (25.15.2).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15.E2

    Used in From one ramp to a logarithmic derivative

  3. Dirichlet nonvanishing at one

    For every nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ the continuation of L(s,χ) is holomorphic at 1 and L(1,χ) is nonzero.

    This makes L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ) a finite centering constant. The principal character requires the separate pole calculation.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §25.15(i) and (25.15.9).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15

    Used in Why the correction terms have these signs · Reflect from zero to one.

  4. Removing Euler factors at a larger modulus

    If χ modulo q is induced by χ₀ of conductor d, then L(s,χ) equals L(s,χ₀) times the product of 1−χ₀(p)p⁻ˢ for p dividing q. The identity holds meromorphically.

    At Re s > 0 every added factor is nonzero, so changing level preserves zeros there.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, (25.15.4).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15.E4

    Used in Removing an imprimitive level

  5. Reflection for a primitive Dirichlet character

    For primitive χ of conductor q, put a=0 or 1 according as χ(−1)=1 or −1. The completed function Λ(s,χ)=(q/π)^((s+a)/2)Γ((s+a)/2)L(s,χ) satisfies Λ(s,χ)=εχΛ(1−s,χ̄), where |εχ|=1.

    In the open critical strip the gamma factors are finite and nonzero. A zero on the left therefore gives a zero for the conjugate character on the right.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §25.15(i), primitive functional equation (25.15.5)–(25.15.6).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15.i

    Used in The strip theorem for characters · Reflect from zero to one.

  6. The boundary of the critical strip

    The only zeros of ζ outside 0 < Re s < 1 are the negative even integers. In particular there are no zeros on Re s = 1.

    Once both open halves of the strip have been handled, this identifies the exceptions in the classical statement about all zeros.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §25.10(i).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.10.i

    Used in Which zeros? · Why classical RH excludes the negative even integers

  7. Changing the order of integration

    On two σ-finite measure spaces a nonnegative measurable function has the same integral in either order, possibly infinite. For a complex measurable function, finiteness of the integral of its absolute value makes both iterated integrals exist almost everywhere and gives the same value. One may take the completed measures.

    In the Mellin identity one variable has counting measure. In the theta integral a majorant must first control two noncompact variables.

    Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory, §1.7, Theorem 1.7.18 and Corollary 1.7.23.https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/12/gsm-126-tao5-measure-book.pdf#page=222

    Used in From one ramp to a logarithmic derivative · Change the order.

  8. Cauchy’s estimate for derivatives

    Suppose g is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk of radius R about σ, with |g| ≤ M on the circle. For each k ≥ 0, |g⁽ᵏ⁾(σ)|/k! ≤ M/Rᵏ. This follows by bounding the integrand in Cauchy’s derivative formula and multiplying by the circumference.

    Subtracting the principal part of an isolated pole gives such a g. The estimate quantifies the advantage of the pole when its distance from σ is smaller than R.

    NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §1.9, Cauchy’s integral formula for derivatives, (1.9.31).https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.9.E31

    Used in Two incompatible derivative rates

  9. Uniqueness of analytic continuation

    Two holomorphic functions on a connected open set agree throughout it if they agree on a set having a limit point there. For meromorphic functions the same conclusion follows by removing their poles locally.

    This carries an equality from the half-plane where an integral converges into the region where the continued coefficients are evaluated.

    NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §1.10(ii), Analytic Continuation.https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.10.ii

    Used in One determinant derivative moves the convergence line. · Removing an imprimitive level

  10. Legendre’s formula for a factorial

    For a prime p and integer n ≥ 0, the exponent of p in n! is ∑ⱼ≥₁ ⌊n/pʲ⌋. Each integer from 1 to n contributes once for each power of p that divides it.

    This is the valuation gained when one passes from a Taylor coefficient to a derivative.

    Gennady Eremin, Legendre’s formula and p-adic analysis, §1, formula (1).https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.11902

    Used in Proving the one-variable estimate

  11. Orthogonality of finite characters

    On a finite abelian group the average of a character is 1 for the trivial character and 0 otherwise. Indeed, translating the sum by a group element multiplies it by the value of the character at that element.

    Applying the identity to a subgroup retains exactly the characters trivial on that subgroup in the arithmetic balance.

    Keith Conrad, Characters of Finite Abelian Groups, Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2.https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/grouptheory/charthy.pdf

    Used in Which characters survive?

  12. Orbit–stabilizer counting

    When a finite group G acts on a set, the orbit of x is in bijection with the cosets of its stabilizer. In particular the orbit size divided by |G| equals 1/|Stab(x)|.

    The same pairs can be counted by first fixing a lattice or by first fixing a marked subspace. The reciprocal stabilizer order is the weight in the second count.

    Keith Conrad, Group Actions, Theorem 3.16.https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/grouptheory/gpaction.pdf

    Used in Why average over a genus? · Proof for two factors of rank at least two.

  13. Product formula in a number field

    For nonzero a in a number field, multiply |a|ᵥ over all places, using the normalized absolute values, with the complex modulus squared at a complex place. The product equals 1.

    The scalar and determinant in a rational similitude contribute cancelling local Jacobians over all places.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 7.15.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=114

    Used in Compute what happens on a fibre.

  14. Local classification determines a global Hermitian space

    Let E/F be quadratic over number fields. Two nondegenerate Hermitian spaces over E of the same rank are isometric if their localizations are isometric everywhere. At nonsplit finite places the determinant modulo local norms distinguishes the two classes of a given positive rank. At real places becoming complex one uses the whole signature.

    To represent a given nonzero length in a plane, compare it with a diagonal plane whose first vector has the prescribed length. An isometry carries that vector into the given plane.

    Benedict H. Gross, Incoherent definite spaces and Shimura varieties, §3, especially Theorem 3.1.https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/incoherent.pdf

    Used in Which lengths reach the counting theorem?

  15. Hasse’s norm theorem

    Let L/K be a cyclic extension of number fields. An element of K× that is a norm at every completion is the norm of an element of L×.

    In the dyadic argument the extension is quadratic. A choice of real signs supplies the norm condition at infinity and the ideal calculation supplies it at the finite places.

    J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter VIII, Theorem 3.1.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf#page=243

    Used in How many sign patterns can a dyadic class miss? · Which lengths reach the counting theorem?

  16. Kronecker’s criterion for a root of unity

    A nonzero algebraic integer whose conjugates all have absolute value at most 1 is a root of unity. Its powers have bounded degree and bounded coefficients in their monic minimal polynomials, so two powers coincide.

    A quotient of conjugate generators is a unit. Checking its complex absolute values now restricts the ambiguity to roots of unity.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Proposition 5.5 and Corollary 5.6.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=89

    Used in How many sign patterns can a dyadic class miss? · Which ideal does the cyclotomic element generate?

  17. The logarithmic lattice of units

    In a number field with r real places and s complex places, the logarithms of the units form a full lattice of rank r+s−1 in the product-formula hyperplane. The kernel is the finite group of roots of unity.

    The lattice gives a compact torus when integrating along the center. Its rank also determines how many independent unit directions a determinant can measure.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 5.9 and the preceding description of the logarithmic map.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=90

    Used in Which central directions still need averaging? · Why can the upper-right block be erased on a stabilizer cycle? · What the detecting cycles can miss

  18. The S-unit theorem

    Let S be a finite set of places of a number field containing all its infinite places. The elements with valuation zero outside S form a finitely generated group. Modulo roots of unity it is free abelian of rank |S|−1.

    Allowing denominators at primes above ℓ adds one free direction for each such prime in the generator estimate.

    Paul Fili and Zachary Miner, A generalization of Dirichlet’s S-unit theorem, §1, statement of the S-unit theorem.https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/zminer/dirichlet-thm.pdf

    Used in Counting the generators before bounding the length

  19. Hilbert’s Theorem 90

    In a cyclic field extension F/K generated by γ, an element v of norm one has the form z/γ(z) for some z in F×.

    After two twisted-norm classes yield the same finite data, their ratio has norm one. Writing that ratio as a coboundary gives the descent used in the kernel count.

    J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter II, Corollary 1.23.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf#page=76

    Used in What the detecting cycles can miss

  20. Artin reciprocity and the existence of class fields

    Fix a modulus 𝔪. Let I be the fractional ideals prime to 𝔪, and P the principal ideals whose generators satisfy its congruences and real sign conditions. For every subgroup H with P ⊆ H ⊆ I there is a class field L/K whose Artin map induces I/H ≃ Gal(L/K). A prime outside 𝔪 maps to arithmetic Frobenius.

    For the ordinary ideal class group this gives the Hilbert class field. Prime-ideal classes can therefore be prescribed by choosing Frobenius elements.

    J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter V, Theorems 3.5 and 3.6.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf#page=167

    Used in Which ideal-class characters survive the local conditions? · How to choose the prime in the inverse ideal class

  21. Chebotarev’s density theorem

    For a finite Galois extension L/K and a conjugacy class C in its group G, the unramified primes of K with Frobenius in C have density |C|/|G|. Excluding finitely many primes preserves this density.

    The argument chooses auxiliary primes with a prescribed action. Its extra conditions on residue degree are treated in the cited passages.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 8.31.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=149

    Used in How to choose the prime in the inverse ideal class · Which Frobenius fixes the invariant, and which exchanges the CM roots? · Turning a determinant into a cycle evaluation

  22. The Chinese remainder theorem

    For pairwise comaximal ideals I₁,…,Iₙ in a commutative ring R, reduction identifies R/(I₁⋯Iₙ) with the product of the R/Iⱼ. Thus each compatible list of independent residues is attained.

    Coprime moduli let the prime selection impose several congruences at once. They also let an exponent act independently on different primary parts.

    The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.15.4, tag 00DT.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DT

    Used in Finding two primes that work for every required twist · Where the auxiliary layer enters the interior sum · Which degree counts the conjugates, and which degree counts the ideal? · How many common witnesses can two flags have?

  23. Local Tate duality with finite coefficients

    For a finite extension K of ℚₚ, a finite continuous Galois module A and its dual Aᴰ=Hom(A,μ∞), cup product and the local invariant give perfect pairings between Hⁱ(K,A) and H²⁻ⁱ(K,Aᴰ), for 0 ≤ i ≤ 2.

    In degree two the local group order becomes the order of a dual invariant group. This is one of the factors in the localization calculation.

    J. S. Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems, second edition, Part I, §2, Corollary 2.3.https://www.jmilne.org/math/Books/ADTnot.pdf#page=36

    Used in How the finite dualities give a length. · The inverse action and the Tate twist

  24. Poitou–Tate duality for localization

    Let A be a finite Galois module over a number field, unramified outside a finite set S containing the archimedean places and the places dividing |A|. Localization in degree two has cokernel dual to H⁰(K,Aᴰ). At real places the sequence uses modified local cohomology. Write Shaⁱ(A) for the kernel of localization in degree i. There is also a perfect pairing of Sha²(A) with Sha¹(Aᴰ).

    For odd ℓ the archimedean corrections vanish for ℓ-primary coefficients. The cokernel gives the global invariant factor in the localization count. The kernel pairing gives equality of the orders of the two finite locally trivial groups in descent.

    J. S. Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems, second edition, Part I, Theorem 4.10.https://www.jmilne.org/math/Books/ADTnot.pdf#page=65

    Used in How the finite dualities give a length. · The inverse action and the Tate twist

  25. The Chowla–Selberg product over imaginary quadratic ideal classes

    For an imaginary quadratic field of fundamental discriminant D<0, put F(z)=√Im(z) |η(z)|², h=|Cl(K)|, and w=|μ(K)|, the number of roots of unity. Write χᴰ for the quadratic character of D. The product of F over the CM points of the ideal classes equals (4π√|D|)^(−h/2) times the product of Γ(a/|D|)^(wχᴰ(a)/4) for 1 ≤ a ≤ |D|.

    Taking logarithms turns the product into a class mean. The period calculation specifies the additional scaling for lattices whose discriminant has been normalized to one.

    A. Barquero-Sanchez et al., Faltings heights of CM elliptic curves and special Gamma values, §3, (3.2), and Theorem 5.1 at conductor one.https://doi.org/10.1007/s40993-017-0077-7

    Used in Why the root discriminant appears · Take the logarithm of the class product.

  26. Cauchy–Binet for a Gram determinant

    Let X be a complex m by r matrix, m ≥ r. The determinant of X*X is the sum of |det Xᵢ|² over all r-element sets of rows i, where Xᵢ is the corresponding square submatrix. This follows by applying the product formula for determinants of rectangular matrices to X* and X.

    For a basis of a Gaussian plane in four dimensions the six two-row minors therefore measure its determinant. The first two values can be counted exactly.

    Andrew Putman, The Cauchy–Binet formula, Theorem 0.1.https://www3.nd.edu/~andyp/notes/CauchyBinet.pdf

    Used in Count the first two determinants in a four-dimensional Gaussian lattice

  27. Siegel–Weil in the convergent unitary range

    In the unitary dual pair over a quadratic extension of number fields, let the Hermitian target have dimension b and Witt index w, and let the doubled source have split rank a. When b−w>a, the theta integral of the standard Schwartz test converges absolutely. For the associated section of the Siegel induced representation the Eisenstein series is regular at (b−a)/2 and its value equals that integral with the measures of the formula.

    Here a<b, so a target of Witt index zero also lies in this range. Expressing the target integral with probability measure produces the explicit inverse volume in the chapter.

    Shunsuke Yamana, The Siegel–Weil formula for unitary groups, Pacific J. Math. 264 (2013), pp. 236–237, convergence criterion and Theorem 2 in the case m−r>n.https://msp.org/pjm/2013/264-1/pjm-v264-n1-p11-p.pdf#page=4

    Used in When does the theta mean equal an Eisenstein value? · Where the quotient volume comes from

  28. The Rallis inner product formula at first occurrence

    In the unitary case of the cited theorem let n<m≤2n, and let the target have Witt index r≤n. Suppose π is irreducible cuspidal and its theta lifts to the smaller indices in this tower vanish. The pairing of two theta lifts is [E:F] times the value at s=(m−n)/2 of the product L(s+1/2,π×χ)Z*(s), with χ the splitting character attached to the target space V and Z* the normalized doubling integral for the chosen vectors.

    The factorization identifies the global L-value and the normalized local factors. The chapter supplies the formula for its own ranks and follows the measure and vector normalizations at each step of the chain.

    W. T. Gan, Y. Qiu and S. Takeda, The regularized Siegel–Weil formula (the second term identity) and the Rallis inner product formula, §11.6, (11.3), and Theorem 11.4(i).https://arxiv.org/pdf/1207.4709v3#page=54

    Used in Where the quotient volume comes from

  29. Norms in an unramified local extension

    If L/K is a finite unramified extension of nonarchimedean local fields, every unit of K is the norm of a unit of L. The valuation of a norm is a multiple of [L:K]. These two facts characterize the nonzero norms.

    At an inert place of the unramified quadratic extension, even valuation therefore suffices. At a split place the norm sends (x,y) to xy, which attains every nonzero scalar.

    J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter III, Proposition 1.2, with the norm of a uniformizer.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf#page=107

    Used in How many sign patterns can a dyadic class miss?

  30. Lagrange inversion for formal power series

    Over a characteristic-zero field let T(u) have constant coefficient zero and invertible linear coefficient. Write u(T) for its inverse. For any power series H and n≥1, n[Tⁿ]H(u(T))=[uⁿ⁻¹]H′(u)(u/T(u))ⁿ.

    Taking H to be the formal integral of the invariant differential gives λ₂₅=99/1280 on the curve at 5.

    I. M. Gessel, Lagrange Inversion, Theorem 2.1.1, formula (2.1.1).https://people.brandeis.edu/~gessel/homepage/papers/Lagrange.pdf

    Used in The first denominator on a good curve at 5

  31. The von Staudt–Clausen denominator theorem

    For even h≥2, adding 1/p to the Bernoulli number Bₕ for each prime p with p−1 dividing h gives an integer. Each such p occurs just once in the denominator.

    For h≤k, all these primes are at most k+1. A single product of primes therefore clears the denominators in the character sum.

    K. Dilcher, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §24.10(i), (24.10.1).https://dlmf.nist.gov/24.10.i

    Used in Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

  32. Fourier series of the Bernoulli polynomials

    For integer k≥2 and real x in [0,1], the Fourier coefficient of Bₖ at nonzero integer m is −k!/(2πim)ᵏ. The constant coefficient vanishes and the series converges absolutely.

    Pairing the positive and negative frequencies bounds |Bₖ(x)| by 2k!ζ(k)/(2π)ᵏ at once for all x.

    K. Dilcher, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, (24.8.3).https://dlmf.nist.gov/24.8.E3

    Used in Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

  33. Euler’s evaluation of ζ(2)

    The series of reciprocal squares of the positive integers has sum π²/6.

    For k≥2 the sum of reciprocal kth powers is at most ζ(2). Both signs of the frequencies in the Bernoulli series therefore cost at most π²/3<4.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, (25.6.1).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.6.E1

    Used in Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

  34. An elementary upper bound for the product of small primes

    For each integer N≥1 the product of the primes p≤N is at most 4ᴺ. For n≥2 the product over n<p≤2n divides the binomial coefficient (2n−1 choose n), which bounds the cost of doubling the cutoff.

    At N=k+1 this bounds the size of the same integer that clears the Bernoulli denominators.

    A. Granville, The distribution of primes, Appendix E, Lemma E1.1 and Proposition E1.2.https://www.math.mcgill.ca/darmon/courses/10-11/nt/Granville-appendices.pdf

    Used in Why the Bernoulli factor is integral · A single integer controls the primes away from the field degree

  35. Hensel lifting of a simple root

    For a complete discrete valuation ring R, a simple root of a monic polynomial modulo the maximal ideal lifts uniquely to a root in R with that residue.

    At the inert prime p, the derivative 2δ is a unit. The two residue roots of X²+d lift distinctly, which identifies the sign of Frobenius on δ.

    The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.153.9 and the simple-root criterion in §10.153.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04GM

    Used in Which Frobenius fixes the invariant, and which exchanges the CM roots?

  36. Nakayama’s lemma

    If a finitely generated module M over a local ring with maximal ideal 𝔪 satisfies 𝔪M=M, then M is zero. In particular generators modulo 𝔪 lift to generators of M.

    Apply this with 𝔪=(ℓ) to the finite-module quotient in the cokernel comparison. This gives the asserted bound for one additional cyclotomic layer.

    The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.20.1, tag 00DV.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DV

    Used in The cost of one more cyclotomic layer

  37. Minkowski’s bound for an ideal class

    For a number field of degree n and discriminant Δ with r₂ pairs of complex embeddings, every ideal class contains an integral ideal of norm at most (4/π)^(r₂)(n!/nⁿ)√|Δ|. Here the exponent r₂ counts conjugate pairs.

    For ℚ(√−5) only norms one and two need checking. For ℚ(ζ₉) the bound is less than 4.47 and gives a second short list of ideals.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 4.3.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT301.pdf

    Used in Which ideal-class characters survive the local conditions? · Fixed classes and coinvariants in two dimensions

  38. Minkowski’s convex body theorem

    Let Λ be a full lattice in ℝⁿ with covolume V. A convex body symmetric about the origin of volume greater than 2ⁿV contains a nonzero point of Λ.

    The simultaneous bounds at the infinite places describe such a body in the real embedding space. Its volume grows with the denominator exponent, giving a nonzero field element small at every required embedding.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 4.19.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT301.pdf

    Used in Why are the common invariant functions constant?

  39. Shapiro’s lemma for group homology

    For a subgroup H of G and a left ℤH-module M, Hⱼ(G, ℤG⊗ℤH M) is naturally isomorphic to Hⱼ(H,M) in every degree j≥0. The tensor product here is over the group ring of H.

    An orbit of chains gives an induced coefficient module. The lemma replaces its group homology by homology of the stabilizer, where the arithmetic estimates apply.

    C. A. Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, Lemma 6.3.2.https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/weibel/06-group_homology_and_cohomology.pdf

    Used in The extra cost in positive homological degree · Why one coefficient is a unit · Compute the stabilization map from an alternating face map

  40. The Ferrero–Washington theorem

    For every prime ℓ and abelian number field K, the cyclotomic ℤℓ-extension of K has Iwasawa μ-invariant zero.

    The monograph needs a uniform upper bound on the number of generators of the ℓ-class groups of its finite layers. The tower argument reconstructs the class-group consequence used here.

    B. Ferrero and L. C. Washington, The Iwasawa invariant μₚ vanishes for abelian number fields, Annals of Mathematics 109 (1979), 377–395.https://annals.math.princeton.edu/1979/190-2/p05

    Used in What Ferrero–Washington supplies in this proof · Putting the three estimates on one interval

  41. Weyl’s dimension formula

    For integral highest weight λ₁≥⋯≥λₙ, the dimension of the irreducible complex representation of U(n) is ∏_{i<j}(λᵢ−λⱼ+j−i)/(j−i). A common determinant twist leaves every difference unchanged.

    At the real places the product of weight differences can be compared term by term with the Vandermonde factors in the formal degree.

    P. Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory, §5.22, Theorem 5.22.1 and its dimension formula.https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/representationtheorybook.pdf

    Used in How an integral fixes the missing constant · What survives in the quotient of dimensions? · An upper bound for the scale of every word

  42. Schur–Weyl duality on tensor powers

    For a finite-dimensional complex vector space V, every endomorphism of V⊗ᵐ commuting with all g⊗ᵐ for g∈GL(V) is a linear combination of permutations of its m tensor factors.

    The permutations give the trace contractions of the invariant tensors. Their cycles determine the powers acquired under block repetition.

    P. Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory, §§5.18–5.19, the double centralizer and Schur–Weyl duality.https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/representationtheorybook.pdf

    Used in Why do permutations account for every invariant tensor?

  43. Hadamard’s determinant inequality

    The absolute determinant of a complex square matrix is at most the product of the Euclidean lengths of its columns. Applying this after taking a positive definite square root gives the corresponding Gram determinant bound.

    Multiplying the local determinant bounds over the complex embeddings controls the ideal index of a set of short vectors.

    K. Lange, Hadamard’s Determinant Inequality, American Mathematical Monthly 121 (2014), 258–259.https://doi.org/10.4169/amer.math.monthly.121.03.258

    Used in Bound the absolute norm of the determinant. · Find a frame shared by the whole face · How a compact part of the cone supplies a partition everywhere

  44. Stokes’ theorem on a simplex

    On an oriented smooth p-simplex σ, the integral of a smooth (p−1)-form over the alternating boundary of σ equals the integral of its exterior derivative over σ.

    A closed form thus vanishes on boundaries when integrated over chains. Its period depends only on the homology class.

    D. Calegari, Notes on Differential Forms, Theorem 2.1.https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/differential_topology_2016/differential_forms_notes.pdf

    Used in How does a group cocycle become a differential form? · Why does one trace per complex place suffice on the filtered cycles?

  45. Cauchy’s theorem for a finite group

    For a prime ℓ dividing the order of a finite group, the group has an element of order ℓ.

    The exponent bound on the Galois quotient then forces every odd prime dividing its order to divide the fixed level order.

    J. S. Milne, Group Theory, Theorem 4.13.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GTe6.pdf

    Used in When an odd prime divides the field degree

  46. Howe duality for local unitary pairs

    Over a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic different from two, the small theta lift of an irreducible smooth representation for a unitary dual pair is either zero or irreducible. Distinct representations with nonzero lifts have distinct partners.

    This gives the local uniqueness underlying the pairing condition. The row argument separately uses its global pairing hypothesis, positivity of the Gram operator and spanning of the target by orthogonal components.

    W. T. Gan and S. Takeda, A proof of the Howe duality conjecture, Theorem 1.2.https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.1995

    Used in Locating one target type

  47. Sinnott’s separation principle

    Suppose Y₁,…,Yₘ are pairwise multiplicatively independent nontrivial Laurent monomials in independent variables over a field k. If ∑rⱼ(Yⱼ)=0 for rational functions rⱼ over k, every rⱼ is constant.

    This is the independence principle behind the separation argument. The finite group-algebra proof in the chapter supplies the required congruence depth and isolates an individual coefficient.

    W. Sinnott, On a theorem of L. Washington, Astérisque 147–148 (1987), appendix restating Proposition 3.1 of his 1984 paper.https://www.numdam.org/article/AST_1987__147-148__209_0.pdf

    Used in Sinnott’s separation argument.

  48. Siegel’s lower bound on a real exceptional zero

    For every ε>0 there is c(ε)>0 such that a real zero β of a real nonprincipal Dirichlet character of modulus m satisfies 1−β≥c(ε)m⁻ᵋ. The constant is ineffective.

    The progression estimate needs a positive lower bound for the distance of the possible exceptional zero from one. Taking ε=1 gives the coarser scale c/m.

    D. Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, Theorem 12.10.https://dms.umontreal.ca/~koukoulo/documents/publications/primes.pdf

    Used in Why only one quadratic twist can keep a near-one zero

  49. Perron inversion for the ramp

    For c>1 and t>0, the inverse Mellin integral of tˢ/[s(s−1)] along Re s=c, with measure ds/(2πi), is max(t−1,0). The two simple poles at 1 and 0 give the term t−1 for t>1.

    On a line where the Dirichlet series converges absolutely, take t=u/n and sum with coefficients Λ(n)χ(n). This gives the contour representation used to compare two endpoints.

    D. Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, Chapters 5 and 7 on Perron inversion. The stated ramp kernel follows by integrating the step kernel.https://dms.umontreal.ca/~koukoulo/documents/publications/primes.pdf

    Used in How the finite prime sum controls the centered ramp

  50. Digamma values at one and one half

    For ψ=Γ′/Γ, one has ψ(1)=−γ and ψ(1/2)=−γ−2 log 2, where γ is Euler’s constant.

    The logarithmic derivative of the completed odd quadratic L-function contains these two values when reflected between zero and one. Their mean determines the constant in the CM period identity.

    NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §5.4(ii), (5.4.12) and (5.4.13).https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.4.ii

    Used in Reflect from zero to one.

Results in the proof

  1. Classical Riemann hypothesis

    For each complex s with ζ(s)=0, s ≠ −2(n+1) for all natural n, and s ≠ 1, Re s=1/2.

    Read the proof step
  2. Nontrivial zeta zeros

    For each complex s with ζ(s)=0, s ≠ −2(n+1) for all natural n, and s ≠ 1, Re s=1/2.

    Read the proof step
  3. Nonvanishing right of the critical line

    For every positive natural modulus N, every complex Dirichlet character χ mod N and s in ℂ with Re s>1/2, (χ ≠ 1 or s ≠ 1) implies L(s,χ) ≠ 0.

    Used by. Classical reflection with the exceptional integers

    Read the proof step
  4. Zeros of every Dirichlet L-function in the strip

    For every positive natural modulus N, every complex Dirichlet character χ mod N and s in ℂ, if 0 < Re s < 1 and L(s,χ)=0 then Re s=1/2.

    Read the proof step
  5. Zeros of primitive Dirichlet L-functions in the strip

    For every positive natural modulus N and every primitive complex Dirichlet character χ mod N, each zero s with 0 < Re s < 1 has Re s=1/2.

    Read the proof step
  6. Ordered products of edge characters are invariant real cocycles

    For a free abelian group A of finite rank, the homogeneous j-cochain Cα evaluates j real additive characters on successive edge increments and multiplies the resulting scalars, with no factorial. It is invariant and closed.

    Hypotheses. Trivial real coefficients. The affine application uses positive degree j=q+1. Each j-cochain takes j+1 vertices; simultaneous translation of all vertices preserves its value.

    Formulas. additive cup word

    Used by. Every positive-degree cocycle on the free lattice has a finite cup decomposition

    Read the proof step
  7. Every positive-degree cocycle on the free lattice has a finite cup decomposition

    For any j≥1 and any invariant closed c in the real homogeneous complex of a finite-rank free abelian group, c is exactly a finite real linear combination of ordered j-fold cups plus δe for an invariant (j−1)-cochain e.

    Hypotheses. The induction splits P=ℤ×G by prepending a coordinate and uses the full homogeneous tuple complex. A finite integral basis identifies the translation lattice with such a coordinate lattice.

    Formulas. additive two pieces

    Uses. Ordered products of edge characters are invariant real cocycles

    Used by. The cup decomposition extends a polynomial annihilator to every translation class

    Read the proof step
  8. The cup decomposition extends a polynomial annihilator to every translation class

    On the additive group of rectangular integral matrices, if a polynomial Fⱼ(v*) kills the cup words as cochains, applying it to the cup decomposition gives Fⱼ(v*)c=δ(Fⱼ(v*)e).

    Hypotheses. Here v* is pullback by entrywise multiplication by v with the operator in the degree on which it acts. The affine application has a totally complex field and 1≤j≤m<r₂. The concrete Fⱼ(1)≠0 and its vanishing on words are separate arithmetic and eigenvalue inputs.

    Uses. Every positive-degree cocycle on the free lattice has a finite cup decomposition

    Used by. One arithmetic unit separates all positive translation degrees in range

    Read the proof step
  9. One arithmetic unit separates all positive translation degrees in range

    For a totally complex number field and 1≤m<r₂ there exists one unit v whose absolute place products of every total degree from 1 to m differ from one. In each such degree j the action of multiplication by v on the real cohomology of the additive n-by-r matrix lattice is annihilated by a real polynomial F_j with F_j(1)≠0.

    Hypotheses. At complex places use the ordinary complex modulus, one place per conjugate pair. The exponent vectors are nonnegative integral. The additive group of rectangular matrices over the ring of integers is a finite-rank free abelian group. The block sizes n,r do not enter the strict bound m<r₂.

    Uses. The cup decomposition extends a polynomial annihilator to every translation class

    Used by. Stabilizer cycles agree with their block-diagonal images in the same group

  400. Finite Fourier interpolation computes the good Whittaker integral

    The good-place integral equals ∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(1−ε^(M+j)q^(−(2z+n−j))) for Re(z)>n². This expression extends holomorphically to all z, and its value at z₀=(M−n)/2 is the density in WDL-01.

    Hypotheses. Good local data include an integral trace-self-dual lattice, unramified quadratic algebra, unit 2, character of valuation-ring conductor, integral unimodular J and T, and the standard lattice indicator. Both Fourier measures are self-dual for their prescribed pairings. The auxiliary lattice height is vol(L+bL)/vol(L) and appears to the power −(z−z₀).

  407. How the character average and the relevant orbits give termwise vanishing

    For distinct words every nonidentity term with geometric Gram label zero is zero.
